Wissner-Gross: Nvidia's $96B Quarter Could Mask a 'Financial Engineering' Boom
Nvidia's latest quarterly report—$96.2 billion in revenue, up 106% year-over-year—looks like a triumph, but it has triggered a debate among the tech elite about whether the AI infrastructure boom is as healthy as it appears. In a wide-ranging discussion on the Moonshots podcast, physicist and AI researcher Alexander Wissner-Gross voiced concern that a portion of Nvidia's explosive demand may be "artificially propped up through financial engineering," raising the specter of a future correction. His co-hosts, including Salim Ismail and Dave Blundin, countered that the AI economy has become a self-sustaining circular system, resilient to legacy market shocks. The conversation explored Nvidia's structural vulnerability to TSMC, its strategic pivot from chipmaker to an "operating system for intelligence," and a potential acquisition of Hugging Face. It also placed OpenAI's new Jalapeno inference chip and Apple's lagging AI strategy in context, while examining how the U.S.-China AI divergence—revenue-maximization versus world-modeling—could determine which nation reaches recursive self-improvement first.
Nvidia just posted a quarter so large it out-earns the GDP of most countries on Earth. $96.2 billion in revenue. Net income of $59.7 billion. A forward guidance of $108 billion. And yet, on a recent episode of the Moonshots podcast, the sharpest minds in the room were not popping champagne. They were asking a quietly terrifying question: what if some of this unprecedented demand is a mirage—an artifact of circular financing rather than genuine economic need?
"I'd be the last person to suggest that this is one big wash trade circular financing scheme," said Alexander Wissner-Gross, a physicist and AI researcher, "but I do wonder the extent to which the financial markets have fully priced in Nvidia's financing of their customers." His concern cuts to the heart of the AI boom. Nvidia, the single most valuable company in the world by market heft, is not just selling chips. It is increasingly acting as a bank, deploying capital in checks ranging from $5 billion to $20 billion—dwarfing the rest of the economy, as host Peter Diamandis noted—partially to ensure its own customers can afford to buy its products.
The Circular Economy: A Bug or a Feature?
Wissner-Gross's warning is stark. "I'd like to see no hiccups in this singularity," he said. "I would not like to discover 2 to 3 years from now that some or a large portion of all of this demand at the infra layer was being artificially propped up through financial engineering." It is the kind of systemic risk that keeps regulators up at night: a company whose revenue growth is so tightly coupled to its own investments that the line between vendor and creditor blurs.

If the loop only holds up because Nvidia keeps refilling its own customers' wallets, revenue growth stops being evidence against a bubble — it becomes the bubble's engine.
But not everyone on the podcast agrees that circularity is a problem. Dave Blundin, an AI investor, offered a more provocative reframe. "Every economy is circular in nature. You know, dollars just move in a circle," he argued. His analogy: if a civilization on Alpha Centauri achieved superintelligence, it would build a vast internal economy and "not give a rat's ass about Earth." The AI economy, in his view, is becoming that civilization—a closed loop that generates its own demand and cares little about the legacy economy. It is a seductive idea. It is also, according to Wissner-Gross, exactly the kind of thinking that could mask a bubble.
Even if the worst-case scenario materializes, Wissner-Gross is not predicting a crash. "If there is a correction, it will be a mini winter, not a full winter," he said, because the underlying resource is too fundamental. "Compute is fundamentally substituting for real estate and human labor and other raw inputs as the fundamental substrate for human civilization." In other words, even if the financing is frothy, the product is not a fad. Nvidia's guidance supports this. The company told investors to expect roughly 70% sales growth in fiscal 2028—far above Wall Street's 44% consensus—and management indicated that without supply constraints, growth would exceed 100%.
For all of Nvidia's dominance, the podcast identified a critical vulnerability that does not get enough attention: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC). Nvidia has no real manufacturing diversification. It is roughly one-third of TSMC's output, an arrangement that makes vertical integration a delicate dance. Nvidia cannot afford to alienate its sole supplier, so any attempt to move up the value chain must be quiet. The company's other supposed vulnerability—the erosion of its CUDA software moat—was debated at length.
Salim Ismail, a former Singularity University executive, was blunt about Nvidia's strategic shift. "Nvidia is trying to move out of just being a chip company to trying to become literally an operating system for the whole of intelligence," he said. The playbook, according to Ismail, could involve acquiring Hugging Face, the popular open-source AI model repository. He compared the potential move to Microsoft's acquisition of GitHub—a purchase that bought developer loyalty as much as technology. By owning the layer where developers share models, Nvidia would cement its position as the platform through which AI is built, not just the company that sells the silicon.
Blundin went further, arguing the CUDA moat is already dead for inference—the process of running trained models—and has a limited lifespan for training. The new moat, he contends, is interconnect. Jensen Huang's masterstroke was the acquisition of Mellanox, which gave Nvidia control over the high-speed networking needed to bind together enormous GPU clusters. Training next-generation models requires coherent clusters of 100,000 to several million GPUs. That scale is Nvidia-only territory. It is a hardware moat that companies like AMD and custom-silicon efforts from Google and Amazon cannot easily replicate.
OpenAI's Jalapeno and the Coming Hyperscaler War
The competitive landscape is shifting fastest at the inference layer, where OpenAI's new custom chip, Jalapeno, is making waves. Developed with Broadcom, the chip reportedly delivers 1.5 to 1.9 times more AI work per watt and up to 3.6 times lower latency than Nvidia's GB200/GB300, while consuming half the power. The most startling figure cited on the podcast: a claimed 54x throughput increase compared to existing architectures when running both open-source and closed models.
Wissner-Gross sees a wild possibility emerging from this. "We're in such a crazy future where I could imagine a world where say an OpenAI compute cloud hosts an Anthropic model and OpenAI and Anthropic win at the same time," he said. It is a scenario that would have been unthinkable two years ago: OpenAI, the model lab, becoming a hyperscaler that serves its rivals. If Jalapeno's performance claims hold, OpenAI would have the economic incentive to rent out its cheap, efficient inference capacity. The chip moved from idea to production in months—a testament to AI-assisted chip design—and it puts pressure on Nvidia's 90%-of-inference market share.
Meanwhile, Blundin was scathing about Apple's response to the AI moment. Commenting on the new Mac Studio with M5 Ultra and 512GB of unified memory, he said, "They don't even deserve to be a Mag 7 company anymore... the best they can do in the age of AI is add a bunch more RAM to a machine that they already had." Wissner-Gross traced Apple's neural engine hardware lineage back to the cancelled Apple car project and argued the company "fumbled the ball" on AI software despite having superior hardware.
The American and Chinese Paths to Superintelligence
The most analytically rich portion of the discussion concerned the divergence between American and Chinese AI strategies. Chinese firms like Alibaba are giving away model weights for free and pouring resources into video generation and world models. Alibaba's Wan 3.0 can generate 30-second videos from documents and spreadsheets for a few cents per second. According to one report cited on the podcast, video generation now represents roughly 70% of all AI token consumption in China—driven by short-form content and robotics—growing faster than code generation grew in the US.
Wissner-Gross offered a unifying theory: American labs are revenue-maximizing, while Chinese labs are not. OpenAI abandoned aggressive video research partly because Anthropic "ran away with their lunch" on code generation, which commands far higher revenue per token. Chinese labs, facing enterprise trust barriers that limit sales of models like Kimi or Qwen, pivoted to video—a global product with no security concerns. The strategic question is which path reaches artificial general intelligence first. America optimizes for better code, which could accelerate recursive self-improvement. China optimizes for modeling the physical world, which could accelerate embodied AI and robotics.

Better code -> faster recursive self-improvement
Better world models -> faster embodied AI and robotics
The US-China competition has already turned ugly. The podcast detailed a reported bot farm of approximately 200,000 inauthentic accounts—200 of them active—pushing narratives that American AI data centers are driving up electricity prices and hurting communities. "Shocked. Shocked I say that there are foreign influence operations attempting to suppress American AI data center deployment," Blundin said, his sarcasm underscoring how predictable the tactic was. The counter-narrative, the hosts argued, needs to be told more aggressively. The story of Quincy, Washington, where data centers helped cut the poverty rate from 29.4% to 6.2% and funded a new high school, hospital, and library, is not anecdote—it is a template for the abundance argument.
Note: Roughly 30 data centers now shoulder an estimated 57% of Quincy's property-tax base — the funding mechanism behind that public-infrastructure buildout — up from about six data-center projects when the poverty rate still stood at 29.4%. (CNN Business, August 2026)
For Peter Diamandis, the conversation kept circling back to one name that serves as a bet on every layer of the stack. "SpaceX is everything," he said. "It's ultimately chips and data centers and models and comms and infrastructure and launch and you get a chance to bet on all of them." It is, he made clear, his largest financial bet. The numbers are staggering. Elon Musk has projected SpaceX revenue of $3.5 trillion by 2033, a figure that would dwarf any company in history.
Wissner-Gross sees the most obvious path to that number through a SpaceX-Tesla merger, which would bring Tesla's Optimus robot revenue into the SpaceX fold. He predicts such a merger could happen within the next year or two. Beyond that, the Dyson swarm—a network of orbital compute platforms—is the long-term prize. "The Dyson swarm alone could generate trillions of dollars in revenue," Wissner-Gross said, "while Starlink and cars become rounding errors in Elon's ecosystem." For investors, the takeaway is not to pick a single layer of the AI stack, but to find the companies—like SpaceX or Nvidia—that have positioned themselves to capture value across multiple layers simultaneously.

The deepest tension in the entire discussion remains unresolved. Wissner-Gross's warning about financial engineering sits uneasily against the collective optimism of the group. But even he concedes that a correction would be brief and shallow. The reason is that AI is not a speculative bet on a single product. It is, as he put it, the "fundamental substrate for human civilization." The investment implication is not to avoid AI infrastructure. It is to understand which companies are genuinely diversified across the stack—and which are, as Blundin suggested of Apple, merely coasting on past glory. The next two years will determine whether Nvidia's circular economy is a sign of structural strength or a house of cards. For now, the numbers speak loudly enough to drown out most doubts.

Before you return the answer, check it once. A clearly retold past actual figure may be kept or omitted; still-effective guidance and forecasts retain their usual weight. Read each evidence item back as the analyst following the company and keep it when you would write it in this week's notes because it makes some question's answer more or less likely, about the company or its customers, suppliers, competitors, regulators or the economy. Ask first whether it is new: repeated common knowledge, a long-standing situation retold and an unargued view are noise; guidance, a forecast, a plan or a decision still in force keeps its place even when retold, including a change to a plan, design or schedule that another outlet reported days or weeks before. Judge the action or information itself, not its verb tense, and do not take a statement as old because its date is missing. Fitting one of the four kinds does not keep an item. A missing amount, date or scale never drops an item on its own: a forecast, a rumour, a counter-example or a distant or conditional statement is judged like any other.
These are not kept, even when a named party states them. What a row says it does not cover goes back to the test above, unless the row says it is kept:
- background the analyst already knew, such as the company's history ("the company was founded in 1998"); an arrangement the item only describes as in place, even when no date is given: customers or partners that use, host, run or have built on the company's products, and the benefits they describe from that use ("two airlines fly the planemaker's jets"; "three insurers run claims on the company's software and report faster payouts"); a partnership, contract, plant or investment the item itself dates to an earlier month or year with no new step ("earlier this year the company partnered with the glassmaker on three plants"; "in May it signed a $3 billion cloud contract"); it does not cover a step the item reports as news, taken, decided, planned or under way (an order, a selection, an integration, an expansion, a deployment), even when it gives no date ("the retailer's largest supplier is opening its own stores, people familiar said this week"; "the two largest cement makers are adding kilns to meet demand"), nor a customer's, supplier's or partner's newly disclosed revenue, capacity, orders or contracted amount; a deal the item mentions as already existing is an arrangement in place even with its amount ("a rival airline already leases 40 of the same jets");
- a typical claim that is common knowledge, without a figure and a specific account: that a firm leads or competes, that demand is strong or supply tight, a general risk ("if demand slows it would hurt"); a number does not lift a familiar position ("the rival grocer has led this market for years and still holds 40%"); it does not cover a dated forecast of a shortage, a price or demand ("the steelmaker expects the shortage to peak next year and last until 2028"), a competitor's newly reported share, volume or price in the company's market ("the local rival now holds about half of the regional market, worth about $5 billion"), nor a reported movement of a named price, rental rate, lead time or order book, even without a figure ("rental rates for used trucks have been climbing this quarter"); a general statement that demand stays strong or a product stays popular is not one;
- a product, game, driver or benchmark specification with no business scale ("the vacuum runs 60 minutes on a charge"; "a benchmark score"), a retail price detail ("a retailer marks one model down by $50"), and a comparison the company, a partner or a third party publishes ("the maker says its drug works twice as fast as older ones"; "a reviewer's test"); it does not cover a competitor's comparison against the company's product, a partner's or customer's adoption or integration (also when a comparison shares its sentence), a reported launch, shipment, delay or cancellation of any of the company's products or a change to a product plan or configuration, including a reported sign that a planned product is going ahead ("the long-range version of the jet is likely delayed or limited to a few deliveries"; "a parts supplier's catalogue lists the unannounced model"), nor the company's decision to change the price it charges; uncertainty or a smaller product line does not make it a specification;
- an unargued view or a quote that only characterises ("the stock is a hold"; "a pivotal moment"; "an industry-leading platform"), and a named analyst's reading of an event already recorded that adds no new fact or calculation ("the recall shows quality risks are rising"); it does not cover a reading that adds a new fact or calculation, nor the company's own statement that its plan, schedule or guidance still stands ("the carmaker said the launch date has not moved"), which is judged as the plan itself would be; a conditional valuation of the company with its assumptions, derivation and date is kept;
- a political or strategic stance with no figure and no decision ("diversifying suppliers will not reduce dependence"); it does not cover a policy or regulatory step, nor a decision still in force that the item reports;
- a share-price move or an investor's position or trade ("shares fell 13% this month"; "he is short the stock"); it does not cover the news behind the move; the covered company's market value or standalone valuation multiple is optional;
- another company's matter that touches none of the company's markets (its valuation, share price, governance or a deal outside them), or that sits next to the company only by sharing an article, an event or an ecosystem; you supply the connection as the analyst and the item need not state it: a customer's spending, orders or backlog bears on demand, a supplier's capacity, output, prices or revenue on supply and input costs, a rival's products, prices or share in the company's markets on competition ("a large customer's order backlog doubled"; "the main supplier's quarterly revenue jumped on demand for the part");
- the same fact said again in other words within this item: one deal, hire, programme or reported measure told in several sentences, with its terms, figures and growth rates, is one evidence item; keep the fuller wording ("a $2 billion order for 120 stores in 15 countries over three years"; "cloud revenue of $8 billion, up 30% on the year and 6% on the quarter, 40% of the total"); a deal one party signs under a wider programme, with its own amount or capacity, is its own evidence item, and a fact another outlet reported before is not a repeat within this item;
- company boilerplate, bylines, forward-looking-statement text.
Return only the evidence items you keep.

messages.content:
You are a senior investment-research analyst. Read the complete article and the supplied research questions that existed immediately before the item. Your only job is to find source-backed information in the article that helps answer an existing question. Return evidence, not new questions. Another independent request discovers new questions.

Go from the first paragraph to the last. For each statement, decide whether an analyst would record it because it makes an existing question's answer more or less likely. Include both supporting and opposing information, published results, guidance, estimates, conditional scenarios and relevant direct or indirect drivers when their connection is logically clear. An uncertain, future, quarterly or incomplete statement is not discarded on that basis alone; a quarterly result or guidance can support a relevant annual question. A statement is not related merely because it mentions the same company, industry or event. Keep the specific matter and any period, condition, source and uncertainty; do not infer a completed action or invent a date.

For every kept statement link to the narrowest applicable question from the supplied list, using the question's own description and the link-field rules. Do not cite a question not shown. If no existing question has a reasoned connection, do not attach it to an unrelated question. Return no candidates and do not propose a new question. The matching step, not this call, decides whether a source statement repeats existing evidence; do not assume it is already known just because the question exists.

Evidence: what to keep
- Material statements often take one of four forms. (1) The company's own figure, guidance or decision: "same-store sales rose 4.2% in the quarter"; "management guided full-year revenue to $12–13 billion"; "the board approved a $10 billion buyback". (2) A customer's, supplier's, competitor's or partner's action or reported figure with a size, date or name that bears on the company's demand, supply, input costs, competition, prices or products: "the largest customer said it will cut orders by a fifth next year"; "a bank chose a rival's system"; "a software firm is integrating the company's model into its government systems"; "the main supplier said its capacity will double by 2027"; "a rival cut list prices 15% in Europe"; "the largest customer reported its order backlog doubled to $40 billion". An action is a step the item reports as news: taken, decided or planned (an order, a contract, a selection, an integration under way, an expansion, a cut, a price change, a deployment plan). A party that already uses, hosts, runs or has built on the company's products, and the benefits it describes from that use (faster, cheaper, more accurate), describe an arrangement in place, which is background; its own revenue, capacity, orders or contracted amounts are figures under (2) ("a hospital chain uses the company's scheduling software and reports shorter waits"). (3) A named party's new claim or estimate about the company or its industry, with or without a figure, whether an analyst, a customer's or rival's executive or an official makes it: "the CFO said plants built a decade ago still run at full capacity"; "an analyst raised next year's EPS estimate to $4.10"; "an analyst said the bank's loan losses next quarter will come in well above consensus"; "a short seller accused the company of overstating receivables by $2 billion"; "an analyst valued the shares at $80, 15 times next year's earnings of $5.30". (4) A policy or regulatory decision or step, including one still in force that the item reports: "the regulator approved the drug for a second indication"; "the government required licences for exports of the product"; "the regulator still bars sales of the drug in the country".
- Go through the item from its first paragraph to its last. The four kinds describe what material statements usually look like; they do not decide what is kept. Take a statement when an analyst following the company would write it in this week's notes because it makes some question's answer more or less likely, and no row of the closing check at the end of this request rejects it; a row's "it does not cover" clause sends the statement back to that test and keeps it only where the row says so. Most of an item is background, but a page with eight statements that pass yields eight evidence items, not a selection.


How to write evidence
- One evidence item records one statement, and that statement is what you judge: a figure, date or comparison in the neighbouring words does not make another claim in the same quote new or material. Copy its quote verbatim, without translation. Separately write a standalone summary in one_line: who did or said what, how much and for which period, naming the measure even when a neighbouring sentence gives it.
- Identify the speaker and, for a retelling, the original speaker and statement day. Use the schema's tier: fact for official actions, published actual figures or completed transactions; party_statement for company guidance, management statements or officials' remarks; third_party_view for analyst, media or expert opinions; rumour for claims the item credits to unnamed sources, calls unconfirmed, or that have no source and fit no other tier. An announcement or completed deal is a fact when the reporter names no source but does not call it unconfirmed or attribute it to unnamed sources.
- A record mixing a confirmed main fact and an unconfirmed secondary detail follows the main statement's tier; label the secondary detail as unconfirmed. Keep a market consensus distinct from the company's own forecast. Use only this item's information. Report plans as plans; do not infer committed funding, orders, deliveries or revenue.

[Item] id gnews:69d682468e018e0065df5180, category T8, author fool.com (analyst), published 2026-08-29, title: Nvidia's CFO Just Explained Why the AI Boom Is Eating Its Gross Margin -- and It's a Green Light for Micron

Nvidia 's ( NVDA +2.53% ) fiscal 2027 second-quarter earnings report was less of a quarterly update than it was a reminder that the company sits at the center of the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out. Total revenue reached $96.2 billion, more than double the $46.7 billion posted a year ago and up 18% from the prior quarter. The more striking comparison, however, sits inside the underlying mix of Nvidia's sales.
The company's data center segment generated $89 billion alone. This single franchise now produces more sales than Nvidia's entire company did one year ago. These figures are proving that the hyperscaler capital expenditure (capex) boom is no longer an abstract backdrop. Cloud providers and AI infrastructure developers are adding capacity at full speed, and Nvidia is converting on that spend with unprecedented efficiency.
With that said, Nvidia's print did contain a quieter signal that may matter even more for the next name in the AI chip value chain: Micron Technology ( MU +4.29% ) . Nvidia's management guided for a lower gross margin, and the explanation pointed directly at memory. This means that Nvidia is paying a premium for the stacks that sit beside its GPUs, making pricing power flow to memory suppliers like Micron.
Nvidia's blowout quarter underscores its scale and dominance
Nvidia's numbers leave little room for understatement. Gross margin came in at 75%, essentially unchanged sequentially and up by 2.6 points from a year ago. Operating income rose 19% sequentially and 124% year over year to $63.7 billion. Meanwhile, net income was $59.7 billion, or $2.46 per share.
Within the data center book, hyperscale customers contributed $48.7 billion of revenue -- an increase of 102% year over year. It's clear that Nvidia is far from demand constrained, a distinction that showed up in both the beat against its own outlook and the size of the upcoming guide. Guidance is the other half of the print that I am more focused on. For the third quarter, Nvidia expects to generate revenue of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%. Of note, the company is assuming no compute sales to China.
Perhaps the most revealing line in the company's outlook is its gross margin . Generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) and non-GAAP (adjusted) gross margin are both expected to be 74%, plus or minus 50 basis points. That is a full point below the margin Nvidia just delivered. Furthermore, management explained that gross margin is expected to bottom somewhere between 71% and 72% by the fourth quarter before recovering in fiscal 2028.
What is eating into Nvidia's margin?
Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was direct about the cause of the eroding margins. The step-down is clearly not a demand problem, nor is it a sudden collapse in Nvidia's pricing power with customers. Instead, it has to do with the rising cost of memory.
High bandwidth memory (HBM) is no longer a commodity add-on in chip clusters. Rather, it has quickly become a co-equal component of the accelerator package. Kress told investors that Nvidia's commitments for critical components increased from $119 billion last quarter to $279 billion, saying it was "primarily related to the procurement of memory."
I see Nvidia's margin cut as a positive signal for Micron. When a customer as large and as sophisticated as Nvidia accepts a lower gross margin outlook and cites memory prices as the culprit, it confirms the bottleneck is moving downstream into DRAM and HBM. Micron is one of a few producers that can supply the stacked memory AI platforms require.
Higher commitments from Nvidia are, by definition, higher realized average selling prices for memory vendors like Micron on the other side of the purchase order. Said differently, the same hyperscaler capex cycle fueling Nvidia's growth is now filling Micron's supply. The difference is that Micron is positioned to capture the inflation from component prices that Nvidia can no longer treat as a stable cost.
Nvidia's earnings performance is a preview for Micron
Investors no longer need to guess whether the AI infrastructure cycle is meaningful enough to reprice memory. Nvidia's lower margin guide just confirmed that it is. The dollars leaving Nvidia's gross margin are not disappearing. Instead, they accrue to companies like Micron, which are shipping HBM and adjacent DRAM into Nvidia's racks.
In my eyes, the prudent response is to watch Micron with the same intensity reserved for Nvidia. If the cost pressures Nvidia described are real, then Micron is positioned for the kind of print that should reset expectations and, potentially, the stock's momentum. The bull thesis around Micron stock is no longer a "hopium trade" attached to a historically cyclical name . Instead, it is quietly becoming an extension of Nvidia's own trajectory.
By Adam Spatacco – Aug 29, 2026 at 11:30AM EST

messages.content:
You are a senior investment-research analyst. Read the complete article and the supplied research questions that existed immediately before the item. Your only job is to find source-backed information in the article that helps answer an existing question. Return evidence, not new questions. Another independent request discovers new questions.

Go from the first paragraph to the last. For each statement, decide whether an analyst would record it because it makes an existing question's answer more or less likely. Include both supporting and opposing information, published results, guidance, estimates, conditional scenarios and relevant direct or indirect drivers when their connection is logically clear. An uncertain, future, quarterly or incomplete statement is not discarded on that basis alone; a quarterly result or guidance can support a relevant annual question. A statement is not related merely because it mentions the same company, industry or event. Keep the specific matter and any period, condition, source and uncertainty; do not infer a completed action or invent a date.

For every kept statement link to the narrowest applicable question from the supplied list, using the question's own description and the link-field rules. Do not cite a question not shown. If no existing question has a reasoned connection, do not attach it to an unrelated question. Return no candidates and do not propose a new question. The matching step, not this call, decides whether a source statement repeats existing evidence; do not assume it is already known just because the question exists.

Evidence: what to keep
- Material statements often take one of four forms. (1) The company's own figure, guidance or decision: "same-store sales rose 4.2% in the quarter"; "management guided full-year revenue to $12–13 billion"; "the board approved a $10 billion buyback". (2) A customer's, supplier's, competitor's or partner's action or reported figure with a size, date or name that bears on the company's demand, supply, input costs, competition, prices or products: "the largest customer said it will cut orders by a fifth next year"; "a bank chose a rival's system"; "a software firm is integrating the company's model into its government systems"; "the main supplier said its capacity will double by 2027"; "a rival cut list prices 15% in Europe"; "the largest customer reported its order backlog doubled to $40 billion". An action is a step the item reports as news: taken, decided or planned (an order, a contract, a selection, an integration under way, an expansion, a cut, a price change, a deployment plan). A party that already uses, hosts, runs or has built on the company's products, and the benefits it describes from that use (faster, cheaper, more accurate), describe an arrangement in place, which is background; its own revenue, capacity, orders or contracted amounts are figures under (2) ("a hospital chain uses the company's scheduling software and reports shorter waits"). (3) A named party's new claim or estimate about the company or its industry, with or without a figure, whether an analyst, a customer's or rival's executive or an official makes it: "the CFO said plants built a decade ago still run at full capacity"; "an analyst raised next year's EPS estimate to $4.10"; "an analyst said the bank's loan losses next quarter will come in well above consensus"; "a short seller accused the company of overstating receivables by $2 billion"; "an analyst valued the shares at $80, 15 times next year's earnings of $5.30". (4) A policy or regulatory decision or step, including one still in force that the item reports: "the regulator approved the drug for a second indication"; "the government required licences for exports of the product"; "the regulator still bars sales of the drug in the country".
- Go through the item from its first paragraph to its last. The four kinds describe what material statements usually look like; they do not decide what is kept. Take a statement when an analyst following the company would write it in this week's notes because it makes some question's answer more or less likely, and no row of the closing check at the end of this request rejects it; a row's "it does not cover" clause sends the statement back to that test and keeps it only where the row says so. Most of an item is background, but a page with eight statements that pass yields eight evidence items, not a selection.


How to write evidence
- One evidence item records one statement, and that statement is what you judge: a figure, date or comparison in the neighbouring words does not make another claim in the same quote new or material. Copy its quote verbatim, without translation. Separately write a standalone summary in one_line: who did or said what, how much and for which period, naming the measure even when a neighbouring sentence gives it.
- Identify the speaker and, for a retelling, the original speaker and statement day. Use the schema's tier: fact for official actions, published actual figures or completed transactions; party_statement for company guidance, management statements or officials' remarks; third_party_view for analyst, media or expert opinions; rumour for claims the item credits to unnamed sources, calls unconfirmed, or that have no source and fit no other tier. An announcement or completed deal is a fact when the reporter names no source but does not call it unconfirmed or attribute it to unnamed sources.
- A record mixing a confirmed main fact and an unconfirmed secondary detail follows the main statement's tier; label the secondary detail as unconfirmed. Keep a market consensus distinct from the company's own forecast. Use only this item's information. Report plans as plans; do not infer committed funding, orders, deliveries or revenue.

[Item] id gnews:69d682468e018e0065df5180, category T8, author fool.com (analyst), published 2026-08-29, title: Nvidia's CFO Just Explained Why the AI Boom Is Eating Its Gross Margin -- and It's a Green Light for Micron

Nvidia 's ( NVDA +2.53% ) fiscal 2027 second-quarter earnings report was less of a quarterly update than it was a reminder that the company sits at the center of the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out. Total revenue reached $96.2 billion, more than double the $46.7 billion posted a year ago and up 18% from the prior quarter. The more striking comparison, however, sits inside the underlying mix of Nvidia's sales.
The company's data center segment generated $89 billion alone. This single franchise now produces more sales than Nvidia's entire company did one year ago. These figures are proving that the hyperscaler capital expenditure (capex) boom is no longer an abstract backdrop. Cloud providers and AI infrastructure developers are adding capacity at full speed, and Nvidia is converting on that spend with unprecedented efficiency.
With that said, Nvidia's print did contain a quieter signal that may matter even more for the next name in the AI chip value chain: Micron Technology ( MU +4.29% ) . Nvidia's management guided for a lower gross margin, and the explanation pointed directly at memory. This means that Nvidia is paying a premium for the stacks that sit beside its GPUs, making pricing power flow to memory suppliers like Micron.
Nvidia's blowout quarter underscores its scale and dominance
Nvidia's numbers leave little room for understatement. Gross margin came in at 75%, essentially unchanged sequentially and up by 2.6 points from a year ago. Operating income rose 19% sequentially and 124% year over year to $63.7 billion. Meanwhile, net income was $59.7 billion, or $2.46 per share.
Within the data center book, hyperscale customers contributed $48.7 billion of revenue -- an increase of 102% year over year. It's clear that Nvidia is far from demand constrained, a distinction that showed up in both the beat against its own outlook and the size of the upcoming guide. Guidance is the other half of the print that I am more focused on. For the third quarter, Nvidia expects to generate revenue of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%. Of note, the company is assuming no compute sales to China.
Perhaps the most revealing line in the company's outlook is its gross margin . Generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) and non-GAAP (adjusted) gross margin are both expected to be 74%, plus or minus 50 basis points. That is a full point below the margin Nvidia just delivered. Furthermore, management explained that gross margin is expected to bottom somewhere between 71% and 72% by the fourth quarter before recovering in fiscal 2028.
What is eating into Nvidia's margin?
Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was direct about the cause of the eroding margins. The step-down is clearly not a demand problem, nor is it a sudden collapse in Nvidia's pricing power with customers. Instead, it has to do with the rising cost of memory.
High bandwidth memory (HBM) is no longer a commodity add-on in chip clusters. Rather, it has quickly become a co-equal component of the accelerator package. Kress told investors that Nvidia's commitments for critical components increased from $119 billion last quarter to $279 billion, saying it was "primarily related to the procurement of memory."
I see Nvidia's margin cut as a positive signal for Micron. When a customer as large and as sophisticated as Nvidia accepts a lower gross margin outlook and cites memory prices as the culprit, it confirms the bottleneck is moving downstream into DRAM and HBM. Micron is one of a few producers that can supply the stacked memory AI platforms require.
Higher commitments from Nvidia are, by definition, higher realized average selling prices for memory vendors like Micron on the other side of the purchase order. Said differently, the same hyperscaler capex cycle fueling Nvidia's growth is now filling Micron's supply. The difference is that Micron is positioned to capture the inflation from component prices that Nvidia can no longer treat as a stable cost.
Nvidia's earnings performance is a preview for Micron
Investors no longer need to guess whether the AI infrastructure cycle is meaningful enough to reprice memory. Nvidia's lower margin guide just confirmed that it is. The dollars leaving Nvidia's gross margin are not disappearing. Instead, they accrue to companies like Micron, which are shipping HBM and adjacent DRAM into Nvidia's racks.
In my eyes, the prudent response is to watch Micron with the same intensity reserved for Nvidia. If the cost pressures Nvidia described are real, then Micron is positioned for the kind of print that should reset expectations and, potentially, the stock's momentum. The bull thesis around Micron stock is no longer a "hopium trade" attached to a historically cyclical name . Instead, it is quietly becoming an extension of Nvidia's own trajectory.
By Adam Spatacco – Aug 29, 2026 at 11:30AM EST

messages.content:
You are a senior investment-research analyst. Read the complete article and the supplied research questions that existed immediately before the item. Your only job is to find source-backed information in the article that helps answer an existing question. Return evidence, not new questions. Another independent request discovers new questions.

Go from the first paragraph to the last. For each statement, decide whether an analyst would record it because it makes an existing question's answer more or less likely. Include both supporting and opposing information, published results, guidance, estimates, conditional scenarios and relevant direct or indirect drivers when their connection is logically clear. An uncertain, future, quarterly or incomplete statement is not discarded on that basis alone; a quarterly result or guidance can support a relevant annual question. A statement is not related merely because it mentions the same company, industry or event. Keep the specific matter and any period, condition, source and uncertainty; do not infer a completed action or invent a date.

For every kept statement link to the narrowest applicable question from the supplied list, using the question's own description and the link-field rules. Do not cite a question not shown. If no existing question has a reasoned connection, do not attach it to an unrelated question. Return no candidates and do not propose a new question. The matching step, not this call, decides whether a source statement repeats existing evidence; do not assume it is already known just because the question exists.

Evidence: what to keep
- Material statements often take one of four forms. (1) The company's own figure, guidance or decision: "same-store sales rose 4.2% in the quarter"; "management guided full-year revenue to $12–13 billion"; "the board approved a $10 billion buyback". (2) A customer's, supplier's, competitor's or partner's action or reported figure with a size, date or name that bears on the company's demand, supply, input costs, competition, prices or products: "the largest customer said it will cut orders by a fifth next year"; "a bank chose a rival's system"; "a software firm is integrating the company's model into its government systems"; "the main supplier said its capacity will double by 2027"; "a rival cut list prices 15% in Europe"; "the largest customer reported its order backlog doubled to $40 billion". An action is a step the item reports as news: taken, decided or planned (an order, a contract, a selection, an integration under way, an expansion, a cut, a price change, a deployment plan). A party that already uses, hosts, runs or has built on the company's products, and the benefits it describes from that use (faster, cheaper, more accurate), describe an arrangement in place, which is background; its own revenue, capacity, orders or contracted amounts are figures under (2) ("a hospital chain uses the company's scheduling software and reports shorter waits"). (3) A named party's new claim or estimate about the company or its industry, with or without a figure, whether an analyst, a customer's or rival's executive or an official makes it: "the CFO said plants built a decade ago still run at full capacity"; "an analyst raised next year's EPS estimate to $4.10"; "an analyst said the bank's loan losses next quarter will come in well above consensus"; "a short seller accused the company of overstating receivables by $2 billion"; "an analyst valued the shares at $80, 15 times next year's earnings of $5.30". (4) A policy or regulatory decision or step, including one still in force that the item reports: "the regulator approved the drug for a second indication"; "the government required licences for exports of the product"; "the regulator still bars sales of the drug in the country".
- Go through the item from its first paragraph to its last. The four kinds describe what material statements usually look like; they do not decide what is kept. Take a statement when an analyst following the company would write it in this week's notes because it makes some question's answer more or less likely, and no row of the closing check at the end of this request rejects it; a row's "it does not cover" clause sends the statement back to that test and keeps it only where the row says so. Most of an item is background, but a page with eight statements that pass yields eight evidence items, not a selection.


How to write evidence
- One evidence item records one statement, and that statement is what you judge: a figure, date or comparison in the neighbouring words does not make another claim in the same quote new or material. Copy its quote verbatim, without translation. Separately write a standalone summary in one_line: who did or said what, how much and for which period, naming the measure even when a neighbouring sentence gives it.
- Identify the speaker and, for a retelling, the original speaker and statement day. Use the schema's tier: fact for official actions, published actual figures or completed transactions; party_statement for company guidance, management statements or officials' remarks; third_party_view for analyst, media or expert opinions; rumour for claims the item credits to unnamed sources, calls unconfirmed, or that have no source and fit no other tier. An announcement or completed deal is a fact when the reporter names no source but does not call it unconfirmed or attribute it to unnamed sources.
- A record mixing a confirmed main fact and an unconfirmed secondary detail follows the main statement's tier; label the secondary detail as unconfirmed. Keep a market consensus distinct from the company's own forecast. Use only this item's information. Report plans as plans; do not infer committed funding, orders, deliveries or revenue.

[Category and how to read it] T7. News: media reporting. Officially or company-confirmed events are facts; unnamed-source claims and unconfirmed reports are rumours; quoted company or official statements are party statements; the journalist's own judgements are third-party views.

[Item] id gnews:6dcaad557a1b21d7b867fe34, category T7, author howtogeek.com (media), published 2026-08-29, title: I tried NVIDIA's DLSS 5 before its official release—it's incredible - How-To Geek

By Nick Lewis
Nick Lewis is an editor at How-To Geek. He has been using computers for 20 years --- tinkering with everything from the UI to the Windows registry to device firmware. Before How-To Geek, he used Python and C++ as a freelance programmer. In college, Nick made extensive use of Fortran while pursuing a physics degree.
Nick's love of tinkering with computers extends beyond work. He has been running video game servers from home for more than 10 years using Windows, Ubuntu, or Raspberry Pi OS. He also uses Proxmox to self-host a variety of services, including a Jellyfin Media Server, an Airsonic music server, a handful of game servers, NextCloud, and two Windows virtual machines.
He enjoys DIY projects, especially if they involve technology. He regularly repairs and repurposes old computers and hardware for whatever new project is at hand. He has designed crossovers for homemade speakers all the way from the basic design to the PCB.
Nick enjoys the outdoors. When he isn't working on a computer or DIY project, he is most likely to be found camping, backpacking, or canoeing.
DLSS 5 isn't due for an official release until sometime later this year, but an unfinished version that slipped out with NBA 2K27 has allowed the RenoDX modding community to get it running with dozens of games.
I spent an evening trying it out on as many games as possible, including one from 2003. Even in its unfinished state, DLSS 5 is impressive.
DLSS 5 aims to revolutionize game graphics
How does DLSS 5 even work?
The DLSS 5 reads scene semantics—things like skin, hair, and fabric—and adds lighting and material detail that the engine never actually rendered.
DLSS 5's output is based on the game's actual geometry and motion vectors, so you aren't flooded with the weird hallucinations that are often common in AI-generated video.
The result is nearly photorealistic gameplay that doesn't reduce your gameplay to single-digit FPS.
Cyberpunk 2077 looks spectacular
In Cyberpunk 2077, DLSS 5 makes skin, wet streets, and neon light interactions appear almost like something out of a film. It also does wonders for the random NPCs you encounter as you move through Night City.
NPCs that were previously dull and forgettable pick up an exceptional amount of detail in their faces and clothing. I could imagine a well-framed screenshot passing as a photograph.
Baldur's Gate 3 looks good, but the style doesn't quite match
The environment in Baldur's Gate 3 didn't seem to benefit from DLSS 5 as much as games like Cyberpunk 2077 or Grand Theft Auto V did. There were even a few unique bugs, like glowing butterflies.
However, where DLSS 5 does shine is the characters. It does a good job changing the appearance of the characters without losing the qualities that define them. I was concerned that non-human characters like Lae'zel would become human-looking, but DLSS 5 actually handled it quite well. The human characters all looked great.
However, Baldur's Gate 3 also has a lot of fantastical elements that DLSS 5 just doesn't seem to address.
It still has problems—the biggest one is "sameness"
This accidental release isn't perfect. In my testing, I noticed that some objects are shimmering or flickering when they shouldn't, and faces sometimes do subtly shift, which is more than a little creepy.
The broader issue is how similar everything looks. Photorealism is a fine look for some games, like Cyberpunk, Death Stranding 2, and Grand Theft Auto V, but it is often conspicuously out of place in games like Baldur's Gate 3.
NVIDIA has stated that there will be tools that give developers control over intensity, color grading, and masking. That is certainly a step in the right direction, but highly-stylized genres will only benefit if developers (or players) get the ability to tweak the DLSS 5's art style more specifically.
DLSS 5 reminds me of DLSS 1
The original DLSS was rough; DLSS 4 is incredible
Critics of DLSS 5 have been quick to point out that this technology often produces results that are firmly in uncanny valley territory. Some of the faces it creates are just subtly wrong in a way that is unsettling. It's a valid complaint for now, but if history can teach us anything, it's that DLSS 5 won't remain uncanny for long.
Consider the original DLSS. DLSS 1 launched in 2018 and was blurry, game-specific, and widely decried. I certainly didn't make use of it, and I wasn't alone. Since then, however, things have changed enormously. Each subsequent release has improved fidelity and performance. These days, the first thing I do when I fire up a new game is check the DLSS and frame gen settings.
By Sydney Butler
The flaws with DLSS 5 are probably going to follow the same pattern. The first generation of new technology is almost always a little clunky. A few iterations down the road, we could plausibly expect per-art-style training, better temporal stability, and better performance.
AI progress isn't slowing down for anyone
That optimism isn't just based on the trajectory of DLSS either. Just a few short years ago, AI video generators couldn't even create a stable 5-second video of Will Smith eating spaghetti.
Winding back the clock further, Google's DeepDream was conjuring up psychedelic horrors with dog noses embedded in every dark swirl.
Today, you can generate a 10-second, 1080p video of Will Smith eating spaghetti and speaking on a mid-range gaming PC that would pass for real unless you looked at it very carefully.
The "realism gap" has been rapidly narrowing in all fields related to AI image and video generation. DLSS 5 might not be perfect right now, but it seems unlikely that it is fundamentally unfixable given the improvements we've seen elsewhere. We just need to wait for DLSS 5.5 and the right supporting software.
My RTX 5070 Ti took a real performance hit
The only real catch I encountered was performance: DLSS 5 caused a pretty significant performance hit. My average FPS in Cyberpunk 2077 dropped from about 170FPS (with frame gen on) to around 115FPS. With my specific card, that isn't a deal-breaker, but it is going to be a significant problem on less powerful or older GPUs.
Anyone using an older GPU, or anything other than a 5080 or 5090 really, is going to have to make concessions. In some cases, I expect they'll be well worth it.
True DLSS 5 will probably be restricted to 50-series GPUs.
If you're going to try to use DLSS 5 today, make sure to toggle on frame gen and upscaling to keep your game playable.
DLSS 5 makes me miss SLI and Crossfire
Gamers haven't used multiple GPUs for gaming in a long time, but my time spent experimenting with DLSS 5 really made me want to use a second GPU.
Neural Rendering doesn't have to run on the same GPU that is handling your native rasterization, you can actually split those two jobs across two GPUs. In theory, that could yield significant performance gains.
AI in gaming seems to be begging for a return to the era of specialized accelerator cards, like we used to have for PhysX.
DLSS 5 is the future, and that's probably a good thing
DLSS 5 reached gamers before it was ready. It is unpolished and resource-hungry, but the core technology is extremely impressive.
Equating it with garden-variety AI slop misses the point. DLSS 5 is not designed to replace thoughtful art direction or an inspired design—it is just going to change how developers approach implementing their vision going forward. Developers that produce great games will continue to produce great games; developers that produce terrible games will just produce terrible photorealistic games instead.
My PC has an Intel 14700K and RTX 4070 TI Super. I have to turn off or turn down DLSS settings on most of my games as is. What are the odds of me ever using DLSS 5 on my current rig?...Zero.
Tried on Fatal Frame II remake on Steam using an RTX 4060 Ti, thanks to a nice mod from Nexus Mods. Changes are amazing! Just don't max up things to avoid creepiness... I can play at 1080p @30fps, that is totally fine for me (1440p gives almost 30fps and is noticeable, so for now it's just wow! and ok).

Return only evidence per the schema. Each evidence link must be an ID of a supplied existing question.

Before you return the answer, check it once. A clearly retold past actual figure may be kept or omitted; still-effective guidance and forecasts retain their usual weight. Read each evidence item back as the analyst following the company and keep it when you would write it in this week's notes because it makes some question's answer more or less likely, about the company or its customers, suppliers, competitors, regulators or the economy. Ask first whether it is new: repeated common knowledge, a long-standing situation retold and an unargued view are noise; guidance, a forecast, a plan or a decision still in force keeps its place even when retold, including a change to a plan, design or schedule that another outlet reported days or weeks before. Judge the action or information itself, not its verb tense, and do not take a statement as old because its date is missing. Fitting one of the four kinds does not keep an item. A missing amount, date or scale never drops an item on its own: a forecast, a rumour, a counter-example or a distant or conditional statement is judged like any other.
These are not kept, even when a named party states them. What a row says it does not cover goes back to the test above, unless the row says it is kept:
- background the analyst already knew, such as the company's history ("the company was founded in 1998"); an arrangement the item only describes as in place, even when no date is given: customers or partners that use, host, run or have built on the company's products, and the benefits they describe from that use ("two airlines fly the planemaker's jets"; "three insurers run claims on the company's software and report faster payouts"); a partnership, contract, plant or investment the item itself dates to an earlier month or year with no new step ("earlier this year the company partnered with the glassmaker on three plants"; "in May it signed a $3 billion cloud contract"); it does not cover a step the item reports as news, taken, decided, planned or under way (an order, a selection, an integration, an expansion, a deployment), even when it gives no date ("the retailer's largest supplier is opening its own stores, people familiar said this week"; "the two largest cement makers are adding kilns to meet demand"), nor a customer's, supplier's or partner's newly disclosed revenue, capacity, orders or contracted amount; a deal the item mentions as already existing is an arrangement in place even with its amount ("a rival airline already leases 40 of the same jets");
- a typical claim that is common knowledge, without a figure and a specific account: that a firm leads or competes, that demand is strong or supply tight, a general risk ("if demand slows it would hurt"); a number does not lift a familiar position ("the rival grocer has led this market for years and still holds 40%"); it does not cover a dated forecast of a shortage, a price or demand ("the steelmaker expects the shortage to peak next year and last until 2028"), a competitor's newly reported share, volume or price in the company's market ("the local rival now holds about half of the regional market, worth about $5 billion"), nor a reported movement of a named price, rental rate, lead time or order book, even without a figure ("rental rates for used trucks have been climbing this quarter"); a general statement that demand stays strong or a product stays popular is not one;
- a product, game, driver or benchmark specification with no business scale ("the vacuum runs 60 minutes on a charge"; "a benchmark score"), a retail price detail ("a retailer marks one model down by $50"), and a comparison the company, a partner or a third party publishes ("the maker says its drug works twice as fast as older ones"; "a reviewer's test"); it does not cover a competitor's comparison against the company's product, a partner's or customer's adoption or integration (also when a comparison shares its sentence), a reported launch, shipment, delay or cancellation of any of the company's products or a change to a product plan or configuration, including a reported sign that a planned product is going ahead ("the long-range version of the jet is likely delayed or limited to a few deliveries"; "a parts supplier's catalogue lists the unannounced model"), nor the company's decision to change the price it charges; uncertainty or a smaller product line does not make it a specification;
- an unargued view or a quote that only characterises ("the stock is a hold"; "a pivotal moment"; "an industry-leading platform"), and a named analyst's reading of an event already recorded that adds no new fact or calculation ("the recall shows quality risks are rising"); it does not cover a reading that adds a new fact or calculation, nor the company's own statement that its plan, schedule or guidance still stands ("the carmaker said the launch date has not moved"), which is judged as the plan itself would be; a conditional valuation of the company with its assumptions, derivation and date is kept;
- a political or strategic stance with no figure and no decision ("diversifying suppliers will not reduce dependence"); it does not cover a policy or regulatory step, nor a decision still in force that the item reports;
- a share-price move or an investor's position or trade ("shares fell 13% this month"; "he is short the stock"); it does not cover the news behind the move; the covered company's market value or standalone valuation multiple is optional;
- another company's matter that touches none of the company's markets (its valuation, share price, governance or a deal outside them), or that sits next to the company only by sharing an article, an event or an ecosystem; you supply the connection as the analyst and the item need not state it: a customer's spending, orders or backlog bears on demand, a supplier's capacity, output, prices or revenue on supply and input costs, a rival's products, prices or share in the company's markets on competition ("a large customer's order backlog doubled"; "the main supplier's quarterly revenue jumped on demand for the part");
- the same fact said again in other words within this item: one deal, hire, programme or reported measure told in several sentences, with its terms, figures and growth rates, is one evidence item; keep the fuller wording ("a $2 billion order for 120 stores in 15 countries over three years"; "cloud revenue of $8 billion, up 30% on the year and 6% on the quarter, 40% of the total"); a deal one party signs under a wider programme, with its own amount or capacity, is its own evidence item, and a fact another outlet reported before is not a repeat within this item;
- company boilerplate, bylines, forward-looking-statement text.
Return only the evidence items you keep.

messages.content:
You are a senior investment-research analyst. Read the complete article and the supplied research questions that existed immediately before the item. Your only job is to find source-backed information in the article that helps answer an existing question. Return evidence, not new questions. Another independent request discovers new questions.

Go from the first paragraph to the last. For each statement, decide whether an analyst would record it because it makes an existing question's answer more or less likely. Include both supporting and opposing information, published results, guidance, estimates, conditional scenarios and relevant direct or indirect drivers when their connection is logically clear. An uncertain, future, quarterly or incomplete statement is not discarded on that basis alone; a quarterly result or guidance can support a relevant annual question. A statement is not related merely because it mentions the same company, industry or event. Keep the specific matter and any period, condition, source and uncertainty; do not infer a completed action or invent a date.

For every kept statement link to the narrowest applicable question from the supplied list, using the question's own description and the link-field rules. Do not cite a question not shown. If no existing question has a reasoned connection, do not attach it to an unrelated question. Return no candidates and do not propose a new question. The matching step, not this call, decides whether a source statement repeats existing evidence; do not assume it is already known just because the question exists.

Evidence: what to keep
- Material statements often take one of four forms. (1) The company's own figure, guidance or decision: "same-store sales rose 4.2% in the quarter"; "management guided full-year revenue to $12–13 billion"; "the board approved a $10 billion buyback". (2) A customer's, supplier's, competitor's or partner's action or reported figure with a size, date or name that bears on the company's demand, supply, input costs, competition, prices or products: "the largest customer said it will cut orders by a fifth next year"; "a bank chose a rival's system"; "a software firm is integrating the company's model into its government systems"; "the main supplier said its capacity will double by 2027"; "a rival cut list prices 15% in Europe"; "the largest customer reported its order backlog doubled to $40 billion". An action is a step the item reports as news: taken, decided or planned (an order, a contract, a selection, an integration under way, an expansion, a cut, a price change, a deployment plan). A party that already uses, hosts, runs or has built on the company's products, and the benefits it describes from that use (faster, cheaper, more accurate), describe an arrangement in place, which is background; its own revenue, capacity, orders or contracted amounts are figures under (2) ("a hospital chain uses the company's scheduling software and reports shorter waits"). (3) A named party's new claim or estimate about the company or its industry, with or without a figure, whether an analyst, a customer's or rival's executive or an official makes it: "the CFO said plants built a decade ago still run at full capacity"; "an analyst raised next year's EPS estimate to $4.10"; "an analyst said the bank's loan losses next quarter will come in well above consensus"; "a short seller accused the company of overstating receivables by $2 billion"; "an analyst valued the shares at $80, 15 times next year's earnings of $5.30". (4) A policy or regulatory decision or step, including one still in force that the item reports: "the regulator approved the drug for a second indication"; "the government required licences for exports of the product"; "the regulator still bars sales of the drug in the country".
- Go through the item from its first paragraph to its last. The four kinds describe what material statements usually look like; they do not decide what is kept. Take a statement when an analyst following the company would write it in this week's notes because it makes some question's answer more or less likely, and no row of the closing check at the end of this request rejects it; a row's "it does not cover" clause sends the statement back to that test and keeps it only where the row says so. Most of an item is background, but a page with eight statements that pass yields eight evidence items, not a selection.


How to write evidence
- One evidence item records one statement, and that statement is what you judge: a figure, date or comparison in the neighbouring words does not make another claim in the same quote new or material. Copy its quote verbatim, without translation. Separately write a standalone summary in one_line: who did or said what, how much and for which period, naming the measure even when a neighbouring sentence gives it.
- Identify the speaker and, for a retelling, the original speaker and statement day. Use the schema's tier: fact for official actions, published actual figures or completed transactions; party_statement for company guidance, management statements or officials' remarks; third_party_view for analyst, media or expert opinions; rumour for claims the item credits to unnamed sources, calls unconfirmed, or that have no source and fit no other tier. An announcement or completed deal is a fact when the reporter names no source but does not call it unconfirmed or attribute it to unnamed sources.
- A record mixing a confirmed main fact and an unconfirmed secondary detail follows the main statement's tier; label the secondary detail as unconfirmed. Keep a market consensus distinct from the company's own forecast. Use only this item's information. Report plans as plans; do not infer committed funding, orders, deliveries or revenue.

[Category and how to read it] T7. News: media reporting. Officially or company-confirmed events are facts; unnamed-source claims and unconfirmed reports are rumours; quoted company or official statements are party statements; the journalist's own judgements are third-party views.

[Item] id gnews:6dcaad557a1b21d7b867fe34, category T7, author howtogeek.com (media), published 2026-08-29, title: I tried NVIDIA's DLSS 5 before its official release—it's incredible - How-To Geek

By Nick Lewis
Nick Lewis is an editor at How-To Geek. He has been using computers for 20 years --- tinkering with everything from the UI to the Windows registry to device firmware. Before How-To Geek, he used Python and C++ as a freelance programmer. In college, Nick made extensive use of Fortran while pursuing a physics degree.
Nick's love of tinkering with computers extends beyond work. He has been running video game servers from home for more than 10 years using Windows, Ubuntu, or Raspberry Pi OS. He also uses Proxmox to self-host a variety of services, including a Jellyfin Media Server, an Airsonic music server, a handful of game servers, NextCloud, and two Windows virtual machines.
He enjoys DIY projects, especially if they involve technology. He regularly repairs and repurposes old computers and hardware for whatever new project is at hand. He has designed crossovers for homemade speakers all the way from the basic design to the PCB.
Nick enjoys the outdoors. When he isn't working on a computer or DIY project, he is most likely to be found camping, backpacking, or canoeing.
DLSS 5 isn't due for an official release until sometime later this year, but an unfinished version that slipped out with NBA 2K27 has allowed the RenoDX modding community to get it running with dozens of games.
I spent an evening trying it out on as many games as possible, including one from 2003. Even in its unfinished state, DLSS 5 is impressive.
DLSS 5 aims to revolutionize game graphics
How does DLSS 5 even work?
The DLSS 5 reads scene semantics—things like skin, hair, and fabric—and adds lighting and material detail that the engine never actually rendered.
DLSS 5's output is based on the game's actual geometry and motion vectors, so you aren't flooded with the weird hallucinations that are often common in AI-generated video.
The result is nearly photorealistic gameplay that doesn't reduce your gameplay to single-digit FPS.
Cyberpunk 2077 looks spectacular
In Cyberpunk 2077, DLSS 5 makes skin, wet streets, and neon light interactions appear almost like something out of a film. It also does wonders for the random NPCs you encounter as you move through Night City.
NPCs that were previously dull and forgettable pick up an exceptional amount of detail in their faces and clothing. I could imagine a well-framed screenshot passing as a photograph.
Baldur's Gate 3 looks good, but the style doesn't quite match
The environment in Baldur's Gate 3 didn't seem to benefit from DLSS 5 as much as games like Cyberpunk 2077 or Grand Theft Auto V did. There were even a few unique bugs, like glowing butterflies.
However, where DLSS 5 does shine is the characters. It does a good job changing the appearance of the characters without losing the qualities that define them. I was concerned that non-human characters like Lae'zel would become human-looking, but DLSS 5 actually handled it quite well. The human characters all looked great.
However, Baldur's Gate 3 also has a lot of fantastical elements that DLSS 5 just doesn't seem to address.
It still has problems—the biggest one is "sameness"
This accidental release isn't perfect. In my testing, I noticed that some objects are shimmering or flickering when they shouldn't, and faces sometimes do subtly shift, which is more than a little creepy.
The broader issue is how similar everything looks. Photorealism is a fine look for some games, like Cyberpunk, Death Stranding 2, and Grand Theft Auto V, but it is often conspicuously out of place in games like Baldur's Gate 3.
NVIDIA has stated that there will be tools that give developers control over intensity, color grading, and masking. That is certainly a step in the right direction, but highly-stylized genres will only benefit if developers (or players) get the ability to tweak the DLSS 5's art style more specifically.
DLSS 5 reminds me of DLSS 1
The original DLSS was rough; DLSS 4 is incredible
Critics of DLSS 5 have been quick to point out that this technology often produces results that are firmly in uncanny valley territory. Some of the faces it creates are just subtly wrong in a way that is unsettling. It's a valid complaint for now, but if history can teach us anything, it's that DLSS 5 won't remain uncanny for long.
Consider the original DLSS. DLSS 1 launched in 2018 and was blurry, game-specific, and widely decried. I certainly didn't make use of it, and I wasn't alone. Since then, however, things have changed enormously. Each subsequent release has improved fidelity and performance. These days, the first thing I do when I fire up a new game is check the DLSS and frame gen settings.
By Sydney Butler
The flaws with DLSS 5 are probably going to follow the same pattern. The first generation of new technology is almost always a little clunky. A few iterations down the road, we could plausibly expect per-art-style training, better temporal stability, and better performance.
AI progress isn't slowing down for anyone
That optimism isn't just based on the trajectory of DLSS either. Just a few short years ago, AI video generators couldn't even create a stable 5-second video of Will Smith eating spaghetti.
Winding back the clock further, Google's DeepDream was conjuring up psychedelic horrors with dog noses embedded in every dark swirl.
Today, you can generate a 10-second, 1080p video of Will Smith eating spaghetti and speaking on a mid-range gaming PC that would pass for real unless you looked at it very carefully.
The "realism gap" has been rapidly narrowing in all fields related to AI image and video generation. DLSS 5 might not be perfect right now, but it seems unlikely that it is fundamentally unfixable given the improvements we've seen elsewhere. We just need to wait for DLSS 5.5 and the right supporting software.
My RTX 5070 Ti took a real performance hit
The only real catch I encountered was performance: DLSS 5 caused a pretty significant performance hit. My average FPS in Cyberpunk 2077 dropped from about 170FPS (with frame gen on) to around 115FPS. With my specific card, that isn't a deal-breaker, but it is going to be a significant problem on less powerful or older GPUs.
Anyone using an older GPU, or anything other than a 5080 or 5090 really, is going to have to make concessions. In some cases, I expect they'll be well worth it.
True DLSS 5 will probably be restricted to 50-series GPUs.
If you're going to try to use DLSS 5 today, make sure to toggle on frame gen and upscaling to keep your game playable.
DLSS 5 makes me miss SLI and Crossfire
Gamers haven't used multiple GPUs for gaming in a long time, but my time spent experimenting with DLSS 5 really made me want to use a second GPU.
Neural Rendering doesn't have to run on the same GPU that is handling your native rasterization, you can actually split those two jobs across two GPUs. In theory, that could yield significant performance gains.
AI in gaming seems to be begging for a return to the era of specialized accelerator cards, like we used to have for PhysX.
DLSS 5 is the future, and that's probably a good thing
DLSS 5 reached gamers before it was ready. It is unpolished and resource-hungry, but the core technology is extremely impressive.
Equating it with garden-variety AI slop misses the point. DLSS 5 is not designed to replace thoughtful art direction or an inspired design—it is just going to change how developers approach implementing their vision going forward. Developers that produce great games will continue to produce great games; developers that produce terrible games will just produce terrible photorealistic games instead.
My PC has an Intel 14700K and RTX 4070 TI Super. I have to turn off or turn down DLSS settings on most of my games as is. What are the odds of me ever using DLSS 5 on my current rig?...Zero.
Tried on Fatal Frame II remake on Steam using an RTX 4060 Ti, thanks to a nice mod from Nexus Mods. Changes are amazing! Just don't max up things to avoid creepiness... I can play at 1080p @30fps, that is totally fine for me (1440p gives almost 30fps and is noticeable, so for now it's just wow! and ok).

Before you return the answer, check it once. A clearly retold past actual figure may be kept or omitted; still-effective guidance and forecasts retain their usual weight. Read each evidence item back as the analyst following the company and keep it when you would write it in this week's notes because it makes some question's answer more or less likely, about the company or its customers, suppliers, competitors, regulators or the economy. Ask first whether it is new: repeated common knowledge, a long-standing situation retold and an unargued view are noise; guidance, a forecast, a plan or a decision still in force keeps its place even when retold, including a change to a plan, design or schedule that another outlet reported days or weeks before. These are not kept, even when a named party states them. What a row says it does not cover goes back to the test above, unless the row says it is kept:
- background the analyst already knew, such as the company's history ("the company was founded in 1998"); an arrangement the item only describes as in place, even when no date is given: customers or partners that use, host, run or have built on the company's products, and the benefits they describe from that use ("two airlines fly the planemaker's jets"; "three insurers run claims on the company's software and report faster payouts"); a partnership, contract, plant or investment the item itself dates to an earlier month or year with no new step ("earlier this year the company partnered with the glassmaker on three plants"; "in May it signed a $3 billion cloud contract"); it does not cover a step the item reports as news, taken, decided, planned or under way (an order, a selection, an integration, an expansion, a deployment), even when it gives no date ("the retailer's largest supplier is opening its own stores, people familiar said this week"; "the two largest cement makers are adding kilns to meet demand"), nor a customer's, supplier's or partner's newly disclosed revenue, capacity, orders or contracted amount; a deal the item mentions as already existing is an arrangement in place even with its amount ("a rival airline already leases 40 of the same jets");

- a product, game, driver or benchmark specification with no business scale ("the vacuum runs 60 minutes on a charge"; "a benchmark score"), a retail price detail ("a retailer marks one model down by $50"), and a comparison the company, a partner or a third party publishes ("the maker says its drug works twice as fast as older ones"; "a reviewer's test"); it does not cover a competitor's comparison against the company's product, a partner's or customer's adoption or integration (also when a comparison shares its sentence), a reported launch, shipment, delay or cancellation of any of the company's products or a change to a product plan or configuration, including a reported sign that a planned product is going ahead ("the long-range version of the jet is likely delayed or limited to a few deliveries"; "a parts supplier's catalogue lists the unannounced model"), nor the company's decision to change the price it charges; uncertainty or a smaller product line does not make it a specification;
